newsitem.title: USA: High doses of inhaled steroids linked to glaucoma.
newsitem.headline: High doses of inhaled steroids linked to glaucoma.

text.p: Long-term use of inhaled steroids at high doses -- a new and popular treatment for controlling the lung inflammation that leads to asthma -- may increase the risk of glaucoma, researchers said Tuesday.
The finding came from Royal Victoria Hospital in Montreal and was based on a study of 48,118 patients in Quebec. The use of both nasal and inhaled steroids was studied.

"Both factors, high-dose administration and prolonged continuous duration of use had to be present to elevate the risk," said the report published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association.
"No significant increase was observed in continuous users of low-to-medium doses of inhaled steroids," it added.

The glaucoma risk was 44 percent higher for those who used high doses of inhaled steroids for three months or longer compared to non-users, the study said. No increased risk was found for steroids taking nasally.

Samy Suissa, a researcher to oversaw the project, told Reuters "the very important message is that people should not stop using these drugs. They are very effective for asthma. So see your doctor, get your eyes checked but don't stop using the drugs."

The report said the high doses linked to glaucoma were in the range of 1,500 to 1,600 micrograms a day. The metered doses which come out of cannisters used in bronchial inhalers vary by product, Suissa said, but in general someone taking six to eight puffs a day might be in the high dose range.
Glaucoma is a condition caused by abnormally high pressure from fluid within the eyeball. It can damage the optic nerve and lead to partial or complete vision loss.
The report published Tuesday said steroids may raise the pressure in the eye by making it harder for fluid to flow from the front chamber of the eye.
The study said patients taking high doses of inhaled steroids over several months should be monitored for glaucoma.

Steroids sprayed into the lungs or nose help reduce inflammation caused by allergic reactions but are not believed to carry the risk associated with steroids taken internally and absorbed by the body's system.
